content: Children with congenital heart diseases (CHD) are at a higher risk of contracting COVID-19 and may experience more severe outcomes and complications from the infection. This increased vulnerability is due to their already compromised physiological states and the presence of other co-existing medical conditions associated with CHD. While most children infected with COVID-19 have favorable outcomes, those who require hospitalization are predominantly infants under the age of one and children with pre-existing medical conditions. The most frequently reported underlying conditions include pulmonary diseases such as asthma, congenital heart disease and other cardiovascular disorders, and immunosuppression caused by cancer, its treatments, or high doses of glucocorticoids. Kawasaki disease, a self-limiting vasculitis that affects multiple organs including the skin, mucous membranes, lymph nodes, blood vessels, and the heart, has been observed in increased numbers among COVID-19-positive patients. Although a definitive link between Kawasaki disease and COVID-19 has not yet been established, ongoing research is being conducted to better understand this potential association. Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C) is a severe condition associated with COVID-19. It is characterized by fever lasting 24 hours or more, laboratory evidence of inflammation (e.g., elevated C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, fibrinogen, procalcitonin, d-dimer, ferritin, LDH, or interleukin-6), and involvement of multiple organ systems (e.g., cardiac, renal, respiratory, hematologic, gastrointestinal, dermatologic, or neurological). Routine vaccinations, including those for Hepatitis A and B, should continue to be administered to children and adolescents during the COVID-19 pandemic. Vaccination status should be assessed at every patient visit, and all due or overdue immunizations should be provided unless specific contraindications exist. According to the CDC, routine vaccinations are an essential component of preventive healthcare and should not be delayed due to the pandemic. For infants exposed to hepatitis B virus (HBV), timely administration of hepatitis B immune globulin at birth, completion of the hepatitis B vaccine series, and post-vaccination serologic testing are crucial to prevent HBV transmission.
